analysis.title: Central Banks Watch: Fed Review - Bullish on the economy, still work to do
key_insights: The Fed held the target range at 3.75-4.00% on 28 October, in line with UniCredit's expectations, consensus and market pricing. The vote was 10-2, with Governor Lisa Cook and Cleveland Fed President Beth Hammack dissenting in favour of a 25bp hike.

The FOMC statement was largely unchanged from September except that economic growth was upgraded to "strong" from "solid". Chair Kevin Warsh tied this to upward revisions to 1H26 GDP growth to above 2% annualised and expectations for growth above 3% in 3Q26, supported by double-digit business investment growth.

The Fed sees the investment recovery starting to broaden beyond AI-related spending. With the labour market in equilibrium and initial jobless claims near multi-decade lows, the FOMC can focus on inflation persistence.

Warsh acknowledged that the September hike and policy signals have tightened broader financial conditions, with investors more selective and credit spreads wider. The Fed views this positively because it makes the expansion more durable, but does not regard conditions as outright tight. UniCredit reads this as supporting further policy action.

Warsh said the economy is running hot but not excessively so, inflation expectations are well anchored, and the Fed is not seeking to "throw sand in the gears". UniCredit reads this as consistent with a quarterly pace of hikes, and the new language on the "accumulation of more information" as pointing to a gradual approach.
UniCredit says the FOMC debate is about when to act, not whether to tighten further, and the bar for a 25bp hike in December is very low.

UniCredit's baseline is unchanged rates throughout 2027 as underlying inflation moderates once the energy shock subsides. Risks are skewed toward more tightening because of rising energy prices, strong AI-related capex and supply bottlenecks.
The FOMC keeps eight meetings a year. From 2027 one meeting will be a broad strategy review, and in 2028 two will be, leaving six regular policy meetings.

The productivity and jobs task force holds a hearing on 16 November on technology and productivity, and Warsh plans to attend. The balance sheet task force is expected to present recommendations in early 1Q27, and some task forces will miss the year-end deadline.
